title: Fixed-Width C/C++ Types (uint16_t), volatile ISR Flags and 1 kHz Timer Loops

blocks.x: Bridge from Python to microcontroller C/C++ by computing roll-over-safe tick differences with **fixed-width integers (`uint16_t`)** and replacing blocking `delay()` loops with a deterministic **$1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer Interrupt Service Routine (`ISR`)** using a `volatile` flag.

blocks.x: Idea 1: Fixed-width C/C++ integers (`uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `int16_t`) and modular rollover subtraction

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Wikipedia — Integer (computer science) ("Standard integer types")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_%28computer_science%29) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Integer (computer science)`** and **`Value and representation`**.
**What to skip:** Skip 128-bit mainframe formats.

**Key takeaway:** In Python, integers grow to any size automatically, but in microcontroller C/C++ (`#include <stdint.h>`) every variable has a fixed hardware bit width: `uint8_t` holds $0..255$ ($1\text{ byte}$), `uint16_t` holds $0..65535$ ($2\text{ bytes}$), and signed `int16_t` holds $-32768..+32767$. Like a 4-wheel mechanical odometer that rolls from `65535` back to `0`, unsigned subtraction modulo $2^{16}$ (`(uint16_t)(now - prev)` in C, or `(now - prev) & 0xFFFF` in Python) always gives the exact elapsed ticks across a rollover (`(4 - 65530) & 0xFFFF == 10`).
**Alternative resource:** [MathsIsFun — Binary Number System](https://www.mathsisfun.com/binary-number-system.html) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]` — Review $2^{16} = 65536$.

blocks.x: Idea 2: Hardware timer Interrupt Service Routines ($1\text{ kHz}$ `ISR`), `volatile` flags, and why `delay()` ruins $\Delta t$

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Wikipedia — Interrupt ("Overview" & "Interrupt handler")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interrupt) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Interrupt`** and **`Overview`**.
**What to skip:** Skip PCIe message-signaled interrupts.

**Key takeaway:** Calling `delay(1)` + `Serial.println()` inside `loop()` stretches your loop period $\Delta t$ from $1.0\text{ ms}$ to $6.0+\text{ ms}$ whenever the serial buffer fills up, causing velocity estimates $\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}$ to spike wildly! Instead, a hardware timer peripheral counts clock pulses in silicon and triggers an **Interrupt Service Routine (`ISR`)** at an exact $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$). Any flag shared between an `ISR` and `loop()` (`volatile bool tick_1khz = false;`) **must** use the C keyword **`volatile`** so the compiler never caches the variable in a CPU register and always reads fresh SRAM.

**Alternative resource:** [Wikipedia — Volatile (computer programming)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_%28computer_programming%29) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]` — Read exact headings **`Volatile (computer programming)`** and **`In C and C++`**.

blocks.x: When transitioning from Python to embedded C/C++ firmware, keep this side-by-side translation table in mind for **fixed-width integers (`uint16_t`)**, **`volatile` ISR flags**, and **hardware timer `ISR` loops**:

Why does `delay(1)` ruin control loops? Suppose a motor rotates steadily by $\Delta \theta = 0.020\text{ rad}$ every millisecond. In a deterministic **$1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer `ISR`** ($\Delta t = 0.0010\text{ s}$), measured velocity is $\omega = \frac{0.020}{0.0010} = 20.0\text{ rad/s}$ on every single tick. By contrast, if a slow `Serial.println()` stalls `loop()` so actual elapsed time stretches to $\Delta t_{\text{actual}} = 0.0050\text{ s}$ while your code still divides by nominal $\Delta t_{\text{nom}} = 0.0010\text{ s}$ after the shaft moved $5\times$ farther ($\Delta \theta = 0.100\text{ rad}$), the computed velocity explodes to $100.0\text{ rad/s}$ ($5\times$ false spike!). Keep your `ISR` short, mark shared flags `volatile`, and never call blocking serial prints inside a real-time loop.

blocks.text:
def uint16_tick_delta(now_u16, prev_u16):
    return (now_u16 - prev_u16) & 0xFFFF


def velocity_from_step(true_omega_rad_s, actual_dt_s, assumed_dt_s=0.001):
    d_theta = true_omega_rad_s * actual_dt_s
    return d_theta / assumed_dt_s


def diagnose_uint8_wrap_bug(target_ticks):
    return target_ticks & 0xFF, target_ticks > 255


for prev_t, now_t in [(1000, 1250), (65530, 4)]:
    dt_ticks = uint16_tick_delta(now_t, prev_t)
    print(f"uint16 prev={prev_t:5d}, now={now_t:5d} -> delta={dt_ticks:3d} ticks")

w_isr = velocity_from_step(true_omega_rad_s=20.0, actual_dt_s=0.001, assumed_dt_s=0.001)
w_stalled = velocity_from_step(true_omega_rad_s=20.0, actual_dt_s=0.005, assumed_dt_s=0.001)
u8_val, u8_wrapped = diagnose_uint8_wrap_bug(300)
print(f"1 kHz Timer ISR (dt=1.0 ms): measured omega = {w_isr:.1f} rad/s")
print(f"Blocking Serial stall (dt=5.0 ms): measured omega = {w_stalled:.1f} rad/s (5x JITTER SPIKE!) | uint8(300)={u8_val} (wrapped={u8_wrapped})")

items.x: **Forgetting `volatile` on a variable modified inside an `ISR`:** If you write `bool tick_1khz = false;` without `volatile`, the C++ compiler's `-O2` optimizer sees that `while (!tick_1khz)` never changes `tick_1khz` inside `loop()` and caches `false` in a CPU register forever—hanging your robot at startup! Always write `volatile bool tick_1khz = false;`.

**Calling `Serial.println()` or `delay()` inside an `ISR`:** An `ISR` must finish in a few microseconds. Never put slow serial prints or `delay()` inside the interrupt handler; set a `volatile` flag or copy data into a buffer and let `loop()` handle low-priority logging.

**16-bit unsigned rollover:** A 16-bit hardware microsecond timer (`uint16_t`, range `0..65535`) was at `prev = 65500` and is now at `now = 64` after wrapping around once. How many microseconds elapsed?
**Why `volatile` is mandatory:** What bug occurs in C/C++ if an `ISR` sets `flag = true` and `main()` checks `if (flag)` on a variable declared without `volatile`?

blocks.x: The compiler may optimize away memory reads in `main()` by caching the old value (`false`) in a CPU register, so `main()` **never sees the `ISR` update**.

items.x: Microcontroller C/C++ uses **fixed-width integers** (`uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `int16_t`, `uint32_t`), where unsigned modular subtraction `(now - prev) & 0xFFFF` is immune to counter wrap-around.
A **$1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer `ISR`** guarantees an exact $\Delta t = 1.000\text{ ms}$ control step, and shared `ISR` variables must be declared **`volatile`**.
